claims.text: Replacing traditional EAM reference potentials with an MLIP trained on ab initio solid and liquid configurations near the melting temperature will improve reference-target phase-space overlap.
The same MLIP intervention will decrease thermodynamic-integration path mismatch.
A training set containing diverse ab initio solid and disordered-liquid configurations can represent the relevant high-temperature environments of multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
An MLIP can capture many-body and local-environment effects more effectively than the EAM reference.
Capturing many-body and local-environment effects produces a potential-energy surface closer to the ab initio potential-energy surface.
A closer potential-energy surface match yields closer agreement between the high-dimensional phase spaces sampled by the reference and ab initio models.
Training on both phases incorporates the many atomic configurations characteristic of the high-temperature liquid and corresponding solid.
The phase-inclusive MLIP bridges the gap between simplified EAM interactions and realistic ab initio interactions.
Increased phase-space overlap reduces thermodynamic-integration path error relative to TOR-TILD calculations using traditional EAM references.
The method is applicable to high-entropy alloys having five or more primary components.
The applicable temperature interval extends from near the melting point to approximately 20% above the melting point.
The method is applicable to compositionally homogeneous mixtures for which representative high-temperature configurations can be obtained.
Standard EAM references used in TOR-TILD insufficiently represent the diverse atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid.
The MLIP intervention may reduce integration-path mismatch by approximately 30–50% relative to EAM references.
Reducing integration-path mismatch will improve free-energy estimation accuracy.
Extreme compositional inhomogeneity may limit the MLIP intervention.
Insufficient sampling of ab initio training data, including during rapid phase transitions or far-from-equilibrium conditions, may limit the intervention.
